key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Introduction to Graph Connectivity In graph theory, connectivity is a fundamental concept that describes how well a graph is 'connected'. It helps us understand if it's possible to get from any point in a network to any other point. This lesson will explore connectivity in both undirected and directed graphs, and introduce ways to measure how connected a graph is. Connectedness in Undirected Graphs Defining Connectivity An undirected graph is called connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices of the graph. A key property of a connected graph is that a simple path (a path that does not repeat vertices) exists between any two distinct vertices. If a graph is not connected, it is called disconnected . A disconnected graph is composed of several connected components , which are the maximally connected subgraphs. How Connected is a Graph? While we can classify a graph as simply 'connected', some graphs are more robustly connected than others. We can measure this robustness by identifying critical vertices and edges that, if removed, would disconnect the graph. Cut Vertices and Cut Edges A cut vertex (also known as an articulation point) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components in a graph. A cut edge (also known as a bridge) is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in a graph. A graph that does not have any cut vertices is called a nonseparable graph . Vertex and Edge Connectivity We can quantify the connectivity of a graph more formally: A vertex cut is a set of vertices whose removal makes a graph disconnected. The vertex connectivity , denoted κ(G), is the minimum number of vertices in a vertex cut. An edge cut is a set of edges whose removal makes a graph disconnected. The edge connectivity , denoted λ(G), is the minimum number of edges in an edge cut. Connectedness in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, the direction of the edges matters, leading to two different types of connectivity. Strong and Weak Connectivity A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from any vertex to any other vertex in the graph, respecting the direction of the edges. This means for any two vertices a and b , there is a path from a to b AND a path from b to a . A directed graph is weakly connected if there is a path between any two vertices in the underlying undirected graph (that is, if we ignore the direction of the edges). Every strongly connected graph is also weakly connected, but the reverse is not necessarily true. Summary In this lesson, we explored the concept of graph connectivity. We learned to distinguish between connected and disconnected undirected graphs, and how to measure connectivity using cut vertices, cut edges, vertex connectivity (κ(G)), and edge connectivity (λ(G)). We also defined the two types of connectivity for directed graphs: strong connectivity and weak connectivity.
